question: Which statement best describes Why stream at all?
options: A `loading.tsx` file in a route segment is sugar for wrapping that segment's `page` in a `<Suspense>` boundary automatically. While the async Server Component for that route is fetching, Next streams the `loading.tsx` UI first, giving you an instant route-level skeleton with zero manual Suspense wiring.

With multiple Suspense boundaries, the page resolves progressively: header and nav stream first, then the product grid, then reviews — each filling in as its data arrives. The order is driven by which promises resolve first, not source order, so independent slow regions never queue behind each other.

A `<Suspense>` boundary marks a part of the tree that may not be ready yet. Next renders the `fallback` instantly into the streamed shell, then streams the real content in once the awaited data resolves and swaps it in. Each boundary is an independent streaming unit, so a slow comment list never blocks the article body.

Without streaming, the server must finish rendering the WHOLE page — including the slowest data fetch — before sending any HTML. Streaming flips this: the server flushes the static shell and ready parts immediately, then sends the slow parts as separate chunks over the same response. The user sees meaningful content far sooner, even though total render time is unchanged.
explanation: Without streaming, the server must finish rendering the WHOLE page — including the slowest data fetch — before sending any HTML. question: Which statement best describes loading.tsx?
options: PPR (an evolving Next.js feature) combines a STATIC prerendered shell with STREAMED dynamic holes in a single response. question: Which statement best describes Progressive rendering?
options: Streaming applies to Server Component rendering: async Server Components that `await` data are the natural streaming units. Client Components inside a boundary stream their server-rendered HTML too, then hydrate. You cannot stream past a point that requires a fully-blocking computation outside Suspense — that work blocks the shell.

Streaming improves Time To First Byte because the first byte is the static shell, not the finished page. It also improves First Contentful Paint and perceived speed: the user reads the shell and skeletons immediately instead of staring at a blank tab.
